hero.title: Glyph: A Body for AI
hero.oneLiner: I built a wearable test bed to see what happens when AI leaves the chat window and becomes something you can wear, move, and build on.

context.text: Glyph started in Northwestern's Spring 2026 Product Practicum. My first idea was a wearable test bed for tinkerers. I spoke with people who build things about attachment, feedback, and adding new parts. At the same time, I kept thinking about how AI was getting better while we were still talking to it through a chat box. Glyph brought those two ideas together.

bullets: I built one model to work out the shape, materials, lights, sleeve, and side module.
The clear model uses thermoformed PETG, PETG-GF parts, a black acrylic layer, and three white light filaments.
I built the working demo separately with a Waveshare ESP32-S3 Touch LCD 1.83-inch board and a XIAO nRF52840 Sense Plus.
I got IMU gestures, BLE-HID, air mouse control, telemetry, Wi-Fi and BLE bridges, and Home Assistant lighting control working.
The demo let me point, select, change brightness and color, and confirm with a snap or tap.

decisions.decision: Start with tinkerers
decisions.why: Talking to people who build wearables gave me clear needs: easy attachment, room for new parts, and feedback that makes sense quickly.
decisions.tradeoff: I could not build the full system in one quarter.

decisions.decision: Use Nothing, the company, as the class reference
decisions.why: I liked the clear shells, black and white hardware, useful lights, and the way the products show how they are put together.
decisions.tradeoff: This was my class project. Nothing was only used as a reference and was not involved.

decisions.decision: Build the form and the working demo separately
decisions.why: One model let me make the wearable look right. The other let me test whether the gestures and controls worked.
decisions.tradeoff: The polished shell and the working electronics were not one device.

worked: The conversations with tinkerers made the module and connection ideas much clearer.
Picking Nothing helped me make consistent choices about the shell, lights, and visible parts.
The two models let me show both the physical idea and the working controls.
didnt: The polished model and the working electronics were not combined.
Haptics, EMG, a dense light matrix, a custom PCB, and the full set of modules were not built.
The size and sleeve still need longer wear testing.

outcome.text: For the final, I brought in the polished wearable model and the separate electronics demo. I kept them separate because that was the honest state of the project.
outcome.proof: Two physical models and a live gesture-to-room demo, Spring 2026

reflection.text: AI has enough brains. I wanted to see what happens when you give it a body.

hero.title: FamilySync – JPMorgan Chase Service Design Concept
hero.oneLiner: An agentic payments service for caregivers, designed with JPMorgan Chase through human-centered research and service design.

context.text: This Northwestern EDI service design project, developed with JPMorgan Chase as the partner, started from a broader question than 'where can AI fit in banking?' The opportunity was to explore where agentic systems could take on real coordination work that cuts across family life, money, logistics, and trust. The concept I landed on was FamilySync: a caregiver service that helps families handle messy moments like a sick child, pickup changes, groceries, rides, and shared payments without turning care into a manual operations project. The challenge was to design the service boundary, not just the interface, so that helpful autonomy stayed visible, consent-based, and appropriately constrained.

bullets: Framed the opportunity around family coordination work rather than a generic banking assistant
Designed FamilySync as a service actor that coordinates tasks, permissions, stakeholders, and payments across a shared household system
Mapped the service across the 5 Es structure: learn, set up, use, address problems, and opt out
Prototype-tested autonomy levels such as Preferences, Autonomous, and Ask-each-time across urgent and non-urgent caregiving scenarios
Built visible permission and privacy framing inspired by Apple-style permission tiles and first-person explanations
Modeled backstage logic, handoffs, approvals, and failure states so the concept extended beyond front-end screens
Used agentic tools in the making process by generating HTML UI components, piping them into Figma through MCP, and creating animated deck assets to explain service flows

decisions.decision: Service actor vs chatbot with personality
decisions.why: Shifted the design toward coordination, permissions, and system behavior instead of conversational novelty.
decisions.tradeoff: Made the concept less immediately familiar than a standard assistant interface.

decisions.decision: Shared authority vs single-user optimization
decisions.why: Family actions affect multiple people, so the service needed explicit decision rights and consent logic.
decisions.tradeoff: Introduced more complexity than designing for one account holder alone.

decisions.decision: Configurable autonomy levels vs one default mode
decisions.why: Allowed people to define where the service can act automatically and where it must pause for approval.
decisions.tradeoff: Required careful framing so the setup itself did not become overwhelming.

decisions.decision: Visible privacy explanations vs invisible data collection
decisions.why: Made trust a designed interaction rather than a policy hidden in the background.
decisions.tradeoff: Reduced the amount of silent automation the system could rely on.

worked: Treating agentic AI as service infrastructure made the concept feel materially different from shallow AI feature ideas.
Scenario-card testing grounded trust conversations in specific action boundaries instead of abstract opinions about AI.
The combination of service blueprinting, storytelling, and interaction prototypes made the system legible to reviewers.
didnt: The opportunity space was larger than one quarter, so final scoping still left open questions around segment focus and long-term rollout.

outcome.text: FamilySync became a strong service design concept for how agentic AI could coordinate caregiving logistics without erasing human judgment. The project moved the conversation from 'AI in finance' toward a more useful frame: AI embedded in service infrastructure, where approvals, privacy, and shared authority are designed with as much care as the interface itself.

reflection.text: This project clarified that agentic AI becomes meaningful when it helps carry real coordination load. The value is not talking to an assistant, but preserving trust while reducing the invisible labor around family care.

hero.title: Squad Up — group ordering for McDonald’s
hero.oneLiner: Group ordering across shared digital touchpoints

context.text: Developed with McDonald's through Northwestern EDI, this human-centered design project focused on group ordering: the messy moment where several people want food together, but one person usually ends up collecting texts, remembering edits, checking totals, and fixing the order. We synthesized observations, interviews, and survey responses into journey maps and interaction prototypes. The resulting experience lets people join from a link, add their own items, see who added what, review the group order, and coordinate payment and pickup.

bullets: Mapped the group-ordering journey from invite, join, browse, add item, review, split, and final confirmation
Designed a shared cart model where each item keeps visible ownership instead of becoming an anonymous list
Created invite and join states so friends could enter the order from a lightweight link or QR flow
Explored review readiness cues so the organizer can tell who is done before checkout
Prototyped group cart, participant, and split-payment states using McDonald's visual language from the slide deck
Kept the interface focused on coordination rather than adding chat, feeds, or social noise

decisions.decision: Shared cart ownership vs one combined item list
decisions.why: Made it clear who added each item, which reduces organizer memory work and makes review faster.
decisions.tradeoff: The cart needs more visual structure than a single-user checkout list.

decisions.decision: Invite link flow vs account-heavy collaboration
decisions.why: Let people join quickly without turning a food order into a full social setup process.
decisions.tradeoff: A lightweight invite model needs clear permissions so people understand what they can edit.

decisions.decision: Review readiness vs instant organizer checkout
decisions.why: Helped the organizer avoid checking out before everyone has confirmed their part of the order.
decisions.tradeoff: Adds a coordination step before payment, but prevents more expensive mistakes.

worked: The shared-cart framing made the concept more specific than a generic ordering redesign.
Assigning items to people clarified responsibility without needing chat or comments.
The invite and review states made the organizer role feel lighter and more controllable.
didnt: The prototype still needs stronger edge-case work around someone leaving, changing an item late, or failing to pay.

outcome.text: The result was a group-ordering concept that turns a messy coordination task into a shared cart with visible ownership, lightweight invites, review readiness, and split-oriented checkout. The case study became a focused exercise in designing collaboration inside a quick-service ordering flow.

reflection.text: The useful lesson was that group ordering is not mainly a menu problem. It is a coordination problem: who is in, who picked what, who is ready, and who is paying.

hero.title: Helios – Mechanical Kinetic Lamp
hero.oneLiner: A mechanical lamp that uses gears and physical motion to restore tactile interaction in an otherwise app-driven lighting world.

context.text: Smart lighting has optimized control but removed interaction. Most lamps are reduced to sliders, presets, or voice commands, making light feel passive and disposable. I wanted to design a lamp where changing light felt intentional and physical, something you engage with using your hands, not an app. The constraint was to make the mechanism visible, understandable, and satisfying rather than hidden.

bullets: Fully 3D-printed mechanical lamp body
Ring gear with eight interlinked spur gears
Manual rotary input for controlling light behavior
Integrated LED light source
Gear-driven linkage translating rotation into light modulation
Modular print design requiring minimal supports
CAD files and print-optimized part geometry

decisions.decision: Manual mechanical control vs electronic dimming
decisions.why: Preserved tactile feedback and physical effort as part of the experience.
decisions.tradeoff: Less precise control compared to digital dimming. Not wireless.

decisions.decision: Ring gear architecture vs linear linkage
decisions.why: Allowed synchronized, expressive motion across multiple elements.
decisions.tradeoff: Increased print time and alignment complexity.

decisions.decision: 3D printing vs off-the-shelf components
decisions.why: Enabled full control over form, scale, and mechanical behavior.
decisions.tradeoff: Iteration speed depended on print cycles.

worked: Gear-driven motion made interaction slow, deliberate, and satisfying.
Visible mechanics helped users immediately understand cause and effect.
Print-first design reduced assembly complexity.
didnt: Small tolerance errors amplified across the gear train and required multiple iterations.

outcome.text: Helios resulted in a fully functional kinetic lamp where light is shaped through motion rather than settings. It stands as a proof that mechanical interaction can coexist with modern lighting without relying on software or automation.

reflection.text: Helios reinforced that physical resistance, motion, and visibility can make everyday interactions feel intentional rather than optimized away.

hero.title: Zero - Second Brain AI Assistant
hero.oneLiner: Part Jarvis, part second brain, part slightly over-caffeinated project partner. Zero talks, chats, remembers people and projects, helps me code, generates images, and turns bugs and feature ideas into a build loop.

context.text: Zero started as a question: what would a second brain feel like if it could also talk back? It grew out of my earlier Jarvis home-assistant experiments, but this version is less about shouting commands at devices and more about living with my context. I built it as an experiment, not a packaged product. It combines voice, chat, image generation, personal memory, coding support, home automation, and project tracking into one assistant. The important part is not that it has a lot of tools; it is that it knows when to use them, when to ask, and when to stay out of the way. It remembers people and projects, knows which devices exist in my space, and keeps a SQL-backed trail of tasks, bugs, feature requests, and decisions so the system improves through real use.

bullets: Designed voice and chat as two equal ways to interact: talk when my hands are busy, type when I need precision.
Built four layers of memory: quick preferences, SQL records, semantic search, and active session context.
Stored people, projects, todos, devices, conversations, bugs, and feature ideas in structured records instead of loose chat history.
Built a custom router that decides whether a request is conversation, home control, project lookup, image generation, bug capture, feature planning, or research before it reaches a model.
Added prompt-injection checks and tool permissions around sensitive actions like home devices, calendars, files, and project memory.
Connected Home Assistant so Zero can work with actual rooms, lights, sensors, aliases, and device state.
Created an image generation lab with reusable prompt styles, generated assets, feedback notes, and lightweight versioning.

Built a live coding workspace where Zero can talk to Codex, surface bugs, suggest next features, summarize changes, and bring in a small council of perspectives when a decision needs more than one brain.

decisions.decision: Assistant experiment over product demo
decisions.why: Zero is strongest when it shows how I think through ambiguous AI interaction: what should be automated, what should be confirmed, and what should stay visible to the user.
decisions.tradeoff: The scope is intentionally uneven in places, but every part teaches something about designing useful AI systems.

decisions.decision: Custom router before model calls
decisions.why: Many requests have a clear shape: turn on a light, find a project note, log a bug, create an image, or answer normally. Routing first makes the assistant faster, cheaper, and easier to trust.
decisions.tradeoff: Router logic needs maintenance, especially when a request is ambiguous or combines multiple intents.

decisions.decision: Four-layer memory instead of one giant chat log
decisions.why: Quick memory stores preferences, SQL keeps hard facts auditable, semantic memory finds related old context, and session memory tracks what is happening right now.
decisions.tradeoff: More plumbing to maintain, but each memory layer has a clear job instead of everything becoming one messy prompt.

decisions.decision: Guardrails around tools
decisions.why: An assistant that can touch home devices, files, calendars, and project records needs permission boundaries and prompt-injection defenses, not just better prompts.
decisions.tradeoff: Guardrails add friction, but that friction is part of making the system usable by a real person.

worked: Framing Zero as an experiment made the project easier to explain: it is about designing context-aware assistance, not claiming to ship a universal assistant.
Voice and chat together made the assistant feel more human-centered because each mode fits a different kind of moment.
The Jarvis lineage makes the home-control part feel grounded, but Zero is much more of a second brain than a remote control.
The SQL-backed bug and feature loop turned personal tinkering into a product-minded iteration system.
The live coding workspace makes the project feel useful to me as a developer, not just impressive as an AI demo.
The router made the assistant feel less random because common actions followed predictable paths.
didnt: The project can easily look like a pile of AI features if the story is not tightly edited.
Memory needs clearer user-facing controls so people can see what Zero knows, forget things, and correct records.
Prompt-injection testing has to keep evolving as more tools become available.
Some flows still need better onboarding so a first-time viewer understands what Zero can safely do.

outcome.text: Zero is now my daily second-brain assistant experiment. It talks, chats, generates images, remembers people and projects, helps me code with Codex, controls parts of my home, and keeps a structured loop of bugs, feature ideas, and project decisions. The recruiter signal is not only that I can wire AI tools together; it is that I can turn a messy technical possibility into a human-centered system with memory, permissions, iteration, and visible tradeoffs.

reflection.text: Zero taught me that the hard part of AI product work is not adding another model call. The hard part is shaping context, trust, timing, and feedback so the assistant feels helpful without feeling chaotic. It pushed me to think like a designer, developer, and product owner at the same time.

hero.title: Surya – Kinetic Wall Timepiece
hero.oneLiner: A kinetic wall-mounted timepiece that represents my family across global time zones, opening and closing as they wake and sleep.

context.text: When I moved to the US, I began missing calls with my family because I never knew if they were awake or asleep. Constantly checking time zones on my phone felt disconnected and impersonal. The limitation was clear: screens show time, but not presence. Surya was built to make their daily rhythms visible at a glance.

bullets: Layered laser-cut wooden mandala body (wall-mount) inspired by solar geometry
Set of mechanical flowers (petals) driven by micro-servos
Custom calibration workflow for tuning servo ranges per flower
Control electronics + wiring harness (power distribution + servo control)
Firmware that maps each flower to a family member and syncs motion to that time zone's light cycle
Physical button inputs for instant 'what time is it for them' checks
Assembly files: CAD/laser-cut vectors + enclosure/jig files for alignment and mounting

decisions.decision: Micro DC Motors vs Servo Motors
decisions.why: Micro DC motors allowed smoother, continuous petal motion and finer emotional control without hard positional snapping.
decisions.tradeoff: Lost absolute position feedback, requiring careful mechanical stops and calibration logic.

decisions.decision: Physical Motion vs Screen-Based Display
decisions.why: Movement communicates presence emotionally and peripherally without demanding attention.
decisions.tradeoff: Increased mechanical complexity and longer iteration cycles compared to UI changes.

decisions.decision: Laser-Cut Wood Layers vs 3D-Printed Structure
decisions.why: Layered wood provided warmth, scale, and visual depth aligned with the mandala form.
decisions.tradeoff: Less tolerance for post-build changes compared to reprinting parts.

worked: Slow, continuous motion made the piece feel calm and alive rather than mechanical.
Assigning one flower per family member made the interaction immediately understandable.
The wall-mounted, layered mandala form gave it the presence of a lasting artifact, not a gadget.
didnt: Achieving smooth, synchronized motion across all flowers took far more iteration than expected due to motor and mechanical variance.

outcome.text: Surya became a functioning kinetic wall timepiece that stays in constant sync with my family's day-night cycles across time zones. More than a prototype, it became a personal artifact that made distance legible and emotionally present. The project established my approach to translating abstract feelings into physical interaction, using motion and form instead of screens to communicate meaning.

reflection.text: Surya showed me that slow, ambient motion can communicate availability and care more clearly than explicit information, especially when distance makes timing fragile.

hero.title: Jarvis – Voice-Controlled Smart Home Assistant
hero.oneLiner: A local, voice-controlled smart assistant that triggers real-world actions without relying on cloud-first voice ecosystems.

context.text: Commercial voice assistants felt opaque, slow, and over-scoped. Simple actions required internet dependency, rigid phrasing, and cloud processing. I wanted a system I could fully understand, control, and extend, one that reacted instantly to voice input and integrated directly with my own hardware and automations. The constraint was to keep it lightweight, local-first, and hackable.

bullets: Custom wake-word–based voice recognition system
Embedded hardware running local inference
LED-based visual feedback system
MQTT communication layer
Integration with Home Assistant automations
Physical enclosure and internal wiring
Firmware for voice models, thresholds, and state handling

decisions.decision: Local voice recognition vs cloud APIs
decisions.why: Reduced latency, preserved privacy, and allowed full system control.
decisions.tradeoff: Required careful tuning of models and thresholds.

decisions.decision: Wake-word + command models vs continuous listening
decisions.why: Prevented false triggers and reduced processing load
decisions.tradeoff: Added a two-step interaction.

decisions.decision: MQTT messaging vs direct device control
decisions.why: Enabled scalable, decoupled integration with multiple devices.
decisions.tradeoff: Introduced system-level complexity.

decisions.decision: LED feedback vs audio responses
decisions.why: Provided instant, non-intrusive confirmation without noise.
decisions.tradeoff: Less expressive than speech output.

worked: Local processing made responses feel immediate and reliable.
Visual feedback reduced uncertainty during interaction.
MQTT allowed easy expansion across devices.
didnt: Voice recognition accuracy dropped in noisy environments.

outcome.text: Jarvis became a functional, extensible voice interface for controlling lights, sensors, and automations in my environment. It was selected among the Top 10 projects in an Edge AI & IoT challenge open across ASEAN countries and hosted by Circuit Digest and DigiKey, validating its technical robustness and design clarity.

reflection.text: Jarvis demonstrated how local-first voice systems can outperform cloud assistants for speed, control, and trust when scoped to real environments.

hero.title: Plotter – Speech-to-Draw Machine
hero.oneLiner: A DIY plotter that turns spoken words into plotted drawings by converting speech to text, then text to vector strokes and G-code.

context.text: Most “voice” interfaces stop at transcription. I wanted voice to become a physical output, something you could hold and keep. The trigger was realizing that creative expression is often blocked by software skill and tooling. The constraint was to build a pipeline that felt magical but stayed understandable: speak, preview, plot, without expensive hardware or closed ecosystems.

bullets: DIY XY plotter hardware with pen lift mechanism
Motion control firmware using G-code
Speech-to-text pipeline to capture spoken input
Text-to-vector stroke conversion (line fonts)
G-code generation script for plotting within bounds
Plot preview + settings UI (bounds, scale, font selection)
Calibration routines for origin, scaling, and pen behavior

decisions.decision: Speech-to-text + plotting pipeline vs manual typing
decisions.why: Made creation faster and more accessible, with a “speak it into existence” feel.
decisions.tradeoff: Needed error handling for transcription mistakes.

decisions.decision: Bounds-based scaling near origin vs full-bed auto layout
decisions.why: Ensured predictable output and avoided edge crashes.
decisions.tradeoff: Required users to think in a constrained canvas.

decisions.decision: Servo pen-lift vs third-axis stepper
decisions.why: Simpler mechanics and cheaper implementation for pen up/down.
decisions.tradeoff: More tuning for consistent lift height and timing.

worked: The end-to-end flow (voice → plot) created a strong “physical computing” moment.
Stroke-font rendering produced clean, plotter-friendly paths.
User-defined bounds prevented most mechanical overrun issues.
didnt: Pen-up timing and final-stroke completion were inconsistent and required repeated tuning.

outcome.text: The plotter reliably converted spoken input into plotted text and drawings, producing repeatable physical artifacts from voice. It became a platform for experimenting with typography, constraints, and computational art, not just a one-off build.

reflection.text: This project clarified how a simple pipeline design can turn a familiar input (voice) into a surprising medium (paper), as long as constraints are explicit and controllable.

decisions.why: Allowed quick reconfiguration of pour volumes without rebuilding hardware.

hero.title: The Lawn: A Garden Everyone Tends
hero.oneLiner: A small floating lawn that every visitor to this site shares. Plant weeds, trim them back, and poke the animals. It keeps growing while nobody is looking.

context.text: I wanted my portfolio to have one thing in it that gets better because other people showed up. A game with a score or an ending would not do that. A garden does: you leave something, someone else cuts it back, and the next person finds it different from how you left it.

bullets: Real-time 3D scene in three.js: tens of thousands of wind-blown grass blades, five plant species that each go through four stages, and animals that react when poked.
One shared garden on a Cloudflare Durable Object, so every visitor sees the same plants and the same cut grass.
Nothing ticks on a server. Each plant stores the moment it was planted and its growth is worked out from the clock, so the garden grows while the site is empty.
No accounts and no names. Planting and trimming are rate limited per visitor to keep one person from wrecking the garden.
If the shared garden is offline, the same rules run in the browser and the lawn becomes a private one.

decisions.decision: An idle garden instead of a scored game
decisions.why: There is no win to chase, so the first visit and the hundredth visit both feel fine.
decisions.tradeoff: Nothing pulls a visitor back except curiosity about what changed.

decisions.decision: Work out growth from timestamps instead of running a server timer
decisions.why: It costs nothing while the site is quiet and every visitor sees the same garden at the same moment.
decisions.tradeoff: Clocks have to agree, so the server sends its time and the browser follows that.

worked: A tool that cuts and a tool that plants make two visitors act against each other without any rules to explain.
The scene stays smooth on a laptop by lowering resolution before it drops detail.
didnt: The shared garden needs moderation thinking before it is busy: right now it is only rate limited.
Phones get fewer grass blades and no depth blur.

outcome.text: Playable in the browser. The shared garden turns on once the Worker is deployed.

reflection.text: A portfolio mostly says what I made. This one lets a visitor make something too.

hero.title: Portfolio Website
hero.oneLiner: An evolving portfolio designed, implemented, audited, and refined through a multi-agent AI workflow.

context.text: This website is both a portfolio and an ongoing experiment in AI-mediated making. I set the product direction, visual language, content, and acceptance criteria, then work across Antigravity, Codex, and Claude to plan changes, implement them, critique the result, and verify the live experience. The interesting part is not that AI writes code; it is how a human keeps intent, taste, factual accuracy, and quality control coherent across many agent-assisted iterations.

bullets: React 19 and TypeScript on Vite for a fast, component-driven single-page application
Framer Motion and a custom timeline system for the portfolio's zoom, scroll, and modal interactions
Structured JSON content for project case studies, career history, and writing
A multi-agent workflow spanning Google Antigravity, OpenAI Codex, and Anthropic Claude
Production builds, browser screenshots, keyboard checks, accessibility audits, and performance verification after meaningful changes

decisions.decision: Multi-agent collaboration vs one AI assistant
decisions.why: Different agents are useful for different modes of work: implementation, critique, research, browser verification, and long-running refactors.
decisions.tradeoff: The human has to preserve context, reconcile conflicting suggestions, and remain accountable for the final result.

decisions.decision: Custom interaction system vs a conventional portfolio template
decisions.why: The timeline, cutting-mat hero, and layered project stories make the portfolio itself evidence of product and interaction thinking.
decisions.tradeoff: A distinctive interface demands more testing, performance work, and accessibility care than a standard scrolling site.

worked: Rapid iteration on design and content.
Using multiple agents made critique and verification part of the build loop instead of an afterthought.
Automated builds, screenshots, and browser checks made ambitious interaction changes safer to ship.
didnt: Agent output still drifts without clear product intent, source-of-truth content, and explicit verification.

outcome.text: The result is a responsive portfolio that serves as a living case study in human-agent collaboration. It shows how AI can expand the amount of design, engineering, auditing, and iteration one person can coordinate while keeping authorship grounded in intent and judgment.

reflection.text: Building this portfolio reinforced that the scarce skill in an AI-mediated workflow is not typing code. It is translating intent into constraints, recognizing when the output is wrong, and carrying a coherent point of view through many rounds of implementation and critique.
